Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

This is not a decision about which language matters more; it is about where a short test will show us the most useful problems before we spend time translating the help pages. The release candidate is due for review in three weeks, and the calendar screen is already stable enough to show people, but the instructions under it are still changing. I have about two hours on my schedule tomorrow, and I want to use that time carefully rather than make a meeting just because everyone is available. Well, that is the practical question anyway.

Section one: The choices are, first, ask the French team to review the date order and weekday labels; second, ask the Japanese team to review the compact layout on a narrow phone; and third, spend the hour checking both versions myself against the design notes. I started to say the French team has more experience with dates—no, the useful distinction is that they have already tested this particular picker in the earlier prototype. They reported that the month name stayed visible when the screen was enlarged and that the week began on Monday in the sample account. That makes their feedback easier to compare with the current build, but it may also mean I am asking them to revisit something they have already explained.

The Japanese team has not seen this version yet, and their phones include two common screen widths that our design group uses less often. The current preview has a long button label, and the translated hint might wrap onto a third line. I can imagine the problem from the screenshot, but I cannot tell whether the button is actually hard to use until somebody taps it. In the last planning call, Mika said, “The screen looks calm in the mockup, but the real device is where the spacing gets honest.” I wrote that down because it is a useful reminder, not because it settles the order of the review. The mockup is on my laptop, and the test phone is charging beside the desk.

There are ordinary scheduling details too: the French reviewer is free at ten thirty and has a call at eleven fifteen, while the Japanese team can look at the build after lunch. Our build server sometimes takes twenty minutes to refresh its screenshots, and yesterday it showed an older hint even though the app itself had the new text. If I book the earlier slot, I need to regenerate the preview before ten and check the language switcher after it finishes. If I wait until after lunch, I can compare the two screen widths first, but I may not get a reply until the following morning because of the time difference. Neither option is impossible, and neither has a guaranteed faster answer.

I have a short checklist from the localization guide, though it is more of a practical note than a formal test plan. It says to check the date example, the weekday order, the label length, the screen reader name, and whether the help link stays attached to the picker. I should probably check the example with the seventeenth of October, because that date made the old English layout look crowded. There are also two translated strings in archive.csv that were copied from the previous release, and I do not know yet whether the product team intends to keep them. I could flag those for the reviewers without suggesting replacement wording, since choosing the actual translation is not part of tomorrow's test.

The tempting choice is to do the whole inspection alone because I know where the design notes are and I can move quickly between the emulator and the spreadsheet. Still, that would mostly confirm that the screen matches what I expect. A reviewer may notice that the label sounds formal or that the help link is easy to miss in a way I would overlook after reading it all week. On the other hand, asking both teams at once could produce scattered comments before I know which question I am trying to answer. Last month, three people sent feedback on different builds, and I spent half an hour matching screenshots to version numbers. I would rather avoid repeating that confusion than gather a larger pile of comments.

I could make a small comparison sheet with the build number, device width, locale, date shown, and the exact control each person tried. The sheet should have room for an observation and a screenshot link, but not a box that pushes people to invent a problem. I would also include the question, “What did you expect to happen when you tapped this?” because it asks about the interaction without implying that the current label is wrong. If I send it before the build refresh is complete, I could accidentally attach an outdated image, so the timing matters more than the template. I have not decided whether to use a shared document or a simple message with the fields in order.

There is a small risk in treating the calendar as self-explanatory. A date picker seems familiar until its format changes, and then a person can read the same numbers in a different order. Our sample date is written with the month name in one preview and numerals in another, which makes the comparison less clean than I first thought. I should keep the sample consistent across both locales if the interface permits it, but I need to check whether changing the sample data would also change the accessibility label. That is another reason to ask a reviewer to use the actual build rather than only comment on a picture. I am not sure if the accessibility label is updated from the same string file as the visible hint.

For tomorrow, I think I will prepare the comparison sheet and regenerate the preview before the ten thirty slot. Then I can ask the French reviewer to check the date order and weekday labels while I specifically ask whether this build behaves differently from the prototype. I will keep the Japanese team as the next review rather than asking them to squeeze in a rushed check during their afternoon. That gives me a chance to send them the refreshed narrow screen preview and the same sample date. I am not calling that a final sequence because the first reviewer could uncover a build issue that changes what we need to ask next, and the Japanese team's device feedback may still be the most useful first test if the layout breaks on a narrow screen. For now, the manageable choice is to prepare the material and keep both questions narrow."}]
